idiom_name: pure ES modules returning new objects; the entry point is the shell
implementation_notes: Keep the core in its own module of `export function`s that take plain data and return new objects built with spread/`map`/`filter` - no `fs`, no `fetch`, no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no `console.log` - and pass the current time, ids and already-fetched facts in as arguments; the shell is the entry point (`bin/cli.js`, the Express handler, the worker) that reads the world, calls the core and applies the result. Because JS objects are mutable references, the value discipline must be explicit where references escape: `Object.freeze` (or `structuredClone` at the boundary) for values handed to the core, and return fresh objects instead of editing the arguments. The classic structure of a `Core` class with injected ports is only justified when ports must be swapped at runtime; plain modules cover the usual case, and `import` graph rules (ESLint `no-restricted-imports`) are the cheap boundary check.
pitfalls: A spread (`{...x}`) copies one level: nested objects and arrays stay shared, so 'returning a new object' can still mutate the shell's state - clone at the boundary or keep the values flat.

`Date.now()`, `Math.random()` and `crypto.randomUUID()` inside the core make tests non-deterministic and pass review easily; pass `now`, ids and any seed in, and let the shell inject the already-resolved lookup instead of a callback that queries the database.

An `async` core function returns a `Promise`: the decision is no longer a value, every caller is pulled into the promise chain, and awaiting inside a decision turns a synchronous rule into an interleaving point - keep the core synchronous.
